prompt:
*Setup.* A *knot diagram* is a closed loop in the plane that may cross itself, with a gap left at each crossing to show which arc passes over and which under (only two arcs cross at any point). A *link* diagram consists of several such loops, called *components*; a knot is a link with one component. Two diagrams are *equivalent* if one can be turned into the other by a sequence of the *Reidemeister moves*: R0 (deform the picture in the plane without changing the crossings), RI (add or remove a small kink, a loop with one crossing), RII (slide one strand completely over, or under, another, creating or removing two crossings) and RIII (slide a strand over or under the crossing of two other strands, across a small triangle of three crossings). The moves may be applied to rotated versions of the local pictures. A *knot invariant* (or *link invariant*) is a quantity that is the same for equivalent knots (links). For $i<j$ the result of problem $i$ may be used in problem $j$.

Show that the R-moves imply the first two of the *reverse R-moves* shown in the figure: RI$_2$ (removing a kink of the opposite handedness to the kink of RI) and RIII$_2$ (a version of RIII with a different over/under arrangement of the three crossings). (The remaining reverse moves may be used without proof later.)
answer: RI$_2$: RI then RII. RIII$_2$: RII, RIII, RII.

solutions.title: Sequences of moves
solutions.body:
**RI$_2$.** Start from the diagram with the opposite kink. Use RI (adding a kink) to put a second small kink on the loop, of the handedness that RI allows and placed so that the new kink's strand and the strand of the original loop cross twice with the same strand on top (a bigon). These two crossings are then removed by one RII move, leaving a plain arc with no crossings. So the opposite kink is removable using RI and RII: RI$_2$ follows.

**RIII$_2$.** Starting from the left-hand diagram of RIII$_2$, apply RII to create two new crossings between a pair of strands in the way that turns the configuration into the triangle configuration of RIII; apply RIII to move the third strand across; then apply RII again to remove the two extra crossings. The result is the right-hand diagram of RIII$_2$. So RIII$_2$ follows from RII and RIII. ∎

reviewNote: Figure-based proof: the official solution is a chain of diagrams; the solution here describes the sequence of moves (RI, RII for RI2; RII, RIII, RII for RIII2) in words, so a human should compare with the pictures.

Show that all knot diagrams with one or two crossings are equivalent to the *unknot* $U$, a loop with no crossings. (You may use the reverse RI move of problem 1.)
answer: Each such diagram has a kink that can be removed by RI or its reverse; repeat.

solutions.title: Remove kinks
solutions.body:
Traverse the closed curve and list the crossings in the order they are met; each crossing is met twice. With one crossing the sequence is $aa$; with two crossings it is $aabb$ or $abba$ (the sequence $abab$ cannot occur for a closed curve in the plane, since the loop between the two visits of $a$ would be crossed by the rest of the curve exactly once). In each case some crossing is met twice in a row, so the part of the curve between its two visits is a loop with no other crossing on it, and its interior contains no other part of the curve (the rest of the curve leaves the crossing on the outside of the loop). This loop is a kink, and RI (or its reverse RI$_2$, depending on the handedness) removes it together with the crossing.

After removing it, a diagram with at most one crossing remains, and the same argument removes that last crossing. The result is a crossingless loop, the unknot. ∎

solutions.title: Chain of moves
solutions.body: Start with the complicated second diagram (the one with the long overlapping loops). Apply, in this order: an RII move to remove the two crossings of the overlapping pair of strands; an RIII move to slide the third strand across the remaining crossing; two RI moves to remove the two kinks that appear; another RIII move to pull the last strand across; and finally an R0 move to straighten the picture. The result is the standard three-crossing diagram on the left of the figure. Since each step is a Reidemeister move, the two diagrams are equivalent. ∎

Let the *crossing number* $c(K)$ be the minimal number of crossings of a diagram of the knot $K$, over all diagrams equivalent to a given one. Show that the crossing number is a knot invariant.
answer: Equivalent diagrams have the same set of equivalent diagrams, so the same minimum.

solutions.title: Argument
solutions.body: Suppose diagrams $D$ and $D'$ are equivalent. Then a diagram is equivalent to $D$ iff it is equivalent to $D'$, because equivalence is an equivalence relation (moves can be reversed and composed). So the set of diagrams over which the minimum is taken is the same for $D$ and $D'$, hence $c(D)=c(D')$. ∎

answer: R-moves never cut and rejoin arcs, so they preserve the number of loops.

solutions.title: Argument
solutions.body: Each R-move changes only the crossings inside a small disc, and it does so by moving strands: it does not cut a strand or join two strands. So the set of closed loops is only deformed, and the number of components is unchanged by each move. Equivalent links are connected by a sequence of moves, so they have the same number of components. ∎

prompt:
*Oriented links.* An oriented link has a chosen direction along each component, and the R-moves are applied preserving directions. The *sign* of a crossing between two oriented strands is $+1$ if the direction of the under-strand is obtained from that of the over-strand by a counterclockwise turn of less than $180^\circ$ (the left picture of Figure 6), and $-1$ otherwise (right picture). The *linking number* $\mathrm{Lk}(D)$ of an oriented link diagram $D$ is the sum over all crossings of: $0$ if both arcs of the crossing belong to the same component, and the sign $\pm1$ of the crossing if they belong to different components.

Compute the linking number of the oriented Hopf link and of the oriented Borromean rings shown in the figure (Figure 5(c) and 5(d)); the signs of the crossings are shown in Figure 6.
answer: Hopf link: $2$. Borromean rings: $0$.

solutions.title: Add the signs of the crossings between different components
solutions.body:
The oriented Hopf link has two crossings, both between its two components, and both have the same sign $+1$ (as drawn), so $\mathrm{Lk}=2$. The Borromean rings have six crossings, all between different components: three of sign $+1$ and three of sign $-1$, so $\mathrm{Lk}=0$.

**Answer: Hopf link $2$, Borromean rings $0$**

Show that the linking number is a link invariant.
answer: Check that none of R0, RI, RII, RIII changes the sum of the signs of crossings between different components.

solutions.title: Check each move
solutions.body:
Equivalent diagrams differ by R-moves, so it is enough to show that each move leaves $\mathrm{Lk}$ unchanged. The part of the diagram outside the small disc of the move is unchanged.

- R0 does not change any crossing.
- RI adds or removes one crossing, a self-crossing of one component, which contributes $0$.
- RII adds or removes two crossings between the same two strands. If the strands belong to the same component the contributions are $0$. If they belong to different components, the two crossings have opposite signs (one strand passes over the other twice, and the other strand crosses it in opposite senses at the two crossings), so their contributions cancel.
- RIII involves three crossings. Each of the three crossings keeps its two strands, its over/under information and the orientations, so each keeps its sign; they are only moved. So the sum is unchanged.

Hence $\mathrm{Lk}$ is a link invariant. ∎

*3-colorings.* Color a link diagram using one color for each connected arc (an arc runs from one undercrossing to the next, so at a crossing the over-strand is one arc and the under-strand is two arcs), such that at every crossing the three incident arcs are either all the same color or all different colors. This is called a *3-coloring*, and $\tau(D)$ is the number of 3-colorings of $D$ (using three available colors). For example, the three arcs of the left trefoil knot cannot be colored with two colors, but can be colored with three.

Calculate $\tau$ for the left trefoil knot shown in the figure.

solutions.title: Count colorings
solutions.body:
The left trefoil has three arcs and three crossings, and at each crossing the three incident arcs are the three arcs of the knot. So a coloring is valid iff the three arcs are all the same color or all different colors. All the same: $3$ colorings. All different: $3!=6$ colorings. Two the same and one different is not allowed. So $\tau=3+6=9$.

**Answer: 9**

Show that $\tau(D)$ is a link invariant.
answer: Each R-move gives a bijection between 3-colorings before and after the move.

solutions.title: Colors as elements of Z/3
solutions.body:
Identify the three colors with $0,1,2\in\mathbb Z/3$. At a crossing with over-arc color $o$ and under-arc colors $u,u'$, the condition ``all equal or all distinct'' is equivalent to $o+u+u'\equiv0\pmod 3$ (all equal gives $3o\equiv0$; all distinct gives $0+1+2\equiv0$; two equal and one different would give $2x+y\equiv0$, forcing $y\equiv x$). So the color on the far side of an under-crossing is determined: $u'=2o-u$.

It suffices to show that each R-move gives a bijection between the colorings before and after the move that does not change the colors on the strands leaving the disc of the move. R0 does not change any crossing.

**RI.** In a kink, the arc $a$ passes over the crossing and ends there as the under-strand; the arc $b$ starts there. The condition is $o=a$, $u=a$, $u'=b$ with $u'=2a-a=a$, so $b=a$. The kink forces both arcs to be the same color, so colorings before correspond to colorings after (where $a$ and $b$ are one arc).

**RII.** The over-strand has color $a$ throughout. The under-strand has colors $u$ (before the first crossing), $m=2a-u$ (between), and then $2a-m=u$ after the second crossing. So the colors leaving the disc are $a$ and $u$, the same as in the picture without crossings (two arcs with colors $a$ and $u$), and $m$ is determined. Bijection.

**RIII.** The three strands are top $T$, middle $M$, bottom $B$ (the top passes over both others, the bottom under both). Let $t,m,b$ be their colors entering the disc. $T$ keeps color $t$ and passes over everything. Before the move: $B$ crosses under $M$ first, giving $2m-b$, then under $T$, giving $2t-2m+b$; $M$ goes under $T$ and leaves with $2t-m$. After the move: $B$ first crosses under $T$, giving $2t-b$, then under $M$ which now has color $2t-m$, giving $2(2t-m)-(2t-b)=2t-2m+b$; and $M$ leaves with $2t-m$. In both pictures the outgoing colors are $t$, $2t-m$ and $2t-2m+b$, and the internal arcs are determined by $t,m,b$. Bijection.

Hence $\tau$ is unchanged by every R-move, so it is a link invariant. ∎

The *connect sum* $K_1\#K_2$ of two knots is formed by cutting each in a single place (on an arc, away from crossings) and joining the ends of the two cuts to each other, so that the result is a single knot. Find, with proof, a formula for $\tau(K_1\#K_2)$ in terms of $\tau(K_1)$ and $\tau(K_2)$.
answer: $\tau(K_1\#K_2)=\dfrac13\tau(K_1)\tau(K_2)$

solutions.title: Matching colors on the cut arcs
solutions.body:
Cut both knots in the middle of an arc, $\alpha_1$ in $K_1$ and $\alpha_2$ in $K_2$, and join. In the sum, the two pieces of the new arcs connect an end of $\alpha_1$ to an end of $\alpha_2$ on both sides; each new arc contains half of $\alpha_1$ and half of $\alpha_2$, so a coloring of the sum restricts to a coloring of each knot in which $\alpha_1$ and $\alpha_2$ have the same color. Conversely any pair of colorings of $K_1$ and $K_2$ in which the cut arcs have the same color gives a coloring of the sum. So the colorings of $K_1\#K_2$ correspond to such pairs.

Now, permuting the three colors maps colorings to colorings, so exactly one third of the $\tau(K_1)$ colorings of $K_1$ have the arc $\alpha_1$ of any given color $c$, i.e. $\frac{\tau(K_1)}3$; likewise $\frac{\tau(K_2)}3$ for $K_2$. Summing over the $3$ possible colors $c$: $\tau(K_1\#K_2)=3\cdot\frac{\tau(K_1)}3\cdot\frac{\tau(K_2)}3=\frac{\tau(K_1)\tau(K_2)}3$. ∎

solutions.title: Connect sums of trefoils
solutions.body: Let $T_n$ be the connect sum of $n$ left trefoils. Then $\tau(T_1)=9=3^2$ and $\tau(T_n)=\frac13\tau(T_{n-1})\cdot9=3\tau(T_{n-1})$, so $\tau(T_n)=3^{n+1}$. A *torus link* $T_{p,q}$ is created by placing $p$ string segments from end to end of a cylinder, evenly spaced around its circumference, twisting the cylinder through $\frac qp$ of a full twist, and gluing the two ends of the cylinder together to form a torus, which is then removed, leaving only the string. (The figure shows the construction for $T_{3,3}$.) Determine with proof the number of components of the link $T_{p,q}$. In particular, when is it a knot?
answer: $\gcd(p,q)$ components; it is a knot iff $\gcd(p,q)=1$.

solutions.title: Follow a strand around the torus
solutions.body:
Number the positions of the $p$ strings at the left end of the cylinder $x_0,x_1,\dots,x_{p-1}$ around the circumference. After going once along the cylinder, a string starting at $x_i$ arrives at the position rotated by $2\pi\cdot\frac qp$, which is $x_{i+q}$ (indices mod $p$), and gluing the ends continues it from there. So the components correspond to the orbits of $i\mapsto i+q$ on $\mathbb Z/p$. The orbit of $i$ has size $\frac p{\gcd(p,q)}$ (the smallest $n>0$ with $nq\equiv0\pmod p$). All orbits have this size, so there are $\frac{p}{p/\gcd(p,q)}=\gcd(p,q)$ orbits, i.e. components.

It is a knot (one component) iff $\gcd(p,q)=1$. ∎

*Kauffman bracket.* For an unoriented link diagram $D$ the Kauffman bracket $\langle D\rangle$ is a polynomial in $A,A^{-1}$ defined by: it is invariant under R0 moves; $\langle U\rangle=1$ for the crossingless unknot; $\langle D\sqcup U\rangle=(-A^2-A^{-2})\langle D\rangle$ when a crossingless unknotted loop $U$ is added disjointly; and, at any crossing, $\langle D\rangle=A\langle D_+\rangle+A^{-1}\langle D_-\rangle$ where $D_+$ and $D_-$ are obtained by replacing the crossing by the two smoothings shown in the figure (the over-strand of the crossing is the one going from lower left to upper right; the left smoothing in the figure is the one with coefficient $A$).

Calculate the Kauffman bracket of the Hopf link (Figure 3(b), shown in the picture).
answer: $\langle\text{Hopf}\rangle=-A^4-A^{-4}$

solutions.title: Smooth one crossing
solutions.body:
Let $\delta=-A^2-A^{-2}$. A single kink on a loop has bracket $A\delta+A^{-1}=-A^3$ if its $A$-smoothing separates a loop, and $A+A^{-1}\delta=-A^{-3}$ if its $A$-smoothing does not (the other smoothing then separates the loop). Smoothing one of the two crossings of the Hopf link gives two diagrams of the unknot with one crossing each, one of each kind: $\langle\text{Hopf}\rangle=A\cdot(-A^3)+A^{-1}\cdot(-A^{-3})=-A^4-A^{-4}$.

**Answer: $-A^4-A^{-4}$**

solutions.body:

solutions.title: Compute with the skein relation
solutions.body:
Write $\delta=-A^2-A^{-2}$, let $I$ denote two parallel strands, and $E$ the tangle with a cap and a cup (the strands turned back).

**RI.** A kink with the loop in the $A$-smoothing gives $A\,\delta+A^{-1}=-A^3$ times the plain strand; a kink of the other handedness gives $A+A^{-1}\delta=-A^{-3}$ times the strand. So $\langle D\rangle$ changes by the factor $-A^{3}$ or $-A^{-3}$: the bracket is *not* RI invariant.

**RII.** The tangle with two crossings is $(AI+A^{-1}E)(A^{-1}I+AE)=I+(A^2+A^{-2})E+E\cdot E=I+(A^2+A^{-2}+\delta)E=I$, since $E\cdot E=\delta E$ (a closed loop is created) and $A^2+A^{-2}+\delta=0$. So the bracket is RII invariant.

**RIII.** Write $\sigma_1=A+A^{-1}e_1$ and $\sigma_2=A+A^{-1}e_2$ for crossings between strands $1,2$ and $2,3$ (with the identity on the third strand), where $e_i$ is the cap-cup between strands $i,i+1$; $e_ie_{i\pm1}e_i=e_i$ and $e_i^2=\delta e_i$. Then $\sigma_1\sigma_2\sigma_1=A\sigma_1^2+A^{-1}\sigma_1e_2\sigma_1$ with $\sigma_1^2=A^2+(1-A^{-4})e_1$ and $\sigma_1e_2\sigma_1=A^2e_2+e_1e_2+e_2e_1+A^{-2}e_1$, giving $\sigma_1\sigma_2\sigma_1=A^3+Ae_1+Ae_2+A^{-1}(e_1e_2+e_2e_1)$. This is symmetric in the indices $1,2$, so it equals $\sigma_2\sigma_1\sigma_2$. Hence the bracket is RIII invariant. R0 invariance is part of the definition. ∎

solutions.title: Check each move
solutions.body: R0 does not change any crossing. In RII the two crossings are between the same two strands with the same strand on top, and the other strand crosses it in opposite senses, so the two signs are opposite and cancel. In RIII each of the three crossings keeps its strands, over/under data and orientations, so each keeps its sign. In RI one crossing is added or removed, and it is a kink crossing with sign $+1$ or $-1$, so the writhe changes by $\pm1$. So the writhe is invariant under R0, RII, RIII, but not under RI. ∎

solutions.title: State sum
solutions.body:
Expand $\langle D_1\sqcup D_2\rangle$ by applying the skein relation to all crossings of $D_1$ only: it equals $\sum_sA^{a(s)-b(s)}\langle(k_s\text{ disjoint circles})\sqcup D_2\rangle=\sum_sA^{a(s)-b(s)}\delta^{k_s}\langle D_2\rangle$ where $k_s$ is the number of loops of the state $s$ of $D_1$ and $\delta=-A^2-A^{-2}$. solutions.title: Use the Jones polynomial
solutions.body:
Mirroring flips every crossing, which exchanges the two smoothings in the skein relation (so $A\leftrightarrow A^{-1}$ in the bracket) and negates the writhe. Hence $f_{\overline K}(A)=f_K(A^{-1})$. If $K$ is amphichiral then $K\simeq\overline K$ and, since $f$ is an invariant, $f_K(A)=f_K(A^{-1})$ (the coefficient of $A^k$ equals that of $A^{-k}$). So if $f_K(A)\ne f_K(A^{-1})$, $K$ is chiral.

**The trefoil.** For the left trefoil, $w=-3$ and $\langle D\rangle=A^7-A^3-A^{-5}$ (problem 11), so $f=(-A^3)^3\langle D\rangle=-A^{9}(A^7-A^3-A^{-5})=-A^{16}+A^{12}+A^4$. This is not unchanged under $A\mapsto A^{-1}$ (the exponents $4,12,16$ are all positive), so the trefoil is chiral.

**Answer: use $f(A)$ vs $f(A^{-1})$; the trefoil is chiral.**
